faq.a: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. Baker's yeast is a species called Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and a packet holds billions of dried, resting cells that wake up in warm, wet dough.

faq.q: What does gluten do in bread?
faq.a: Gluten is a protein network that forms when wheat flour is mixed with water and kneaded. It is stretchy, like chewing gum, and traps the gas the yeast makes, so the dough can rise.

faq.q: Why does dough need a warm place to rise?
faq.a: Yeast is alive, and like most living things it works faster when warm, best at around 25 to 35 degrees Celsius. Too hot, around 60 degrees, and the yeast dies.
Yeast makes a little alcohol as well as carbon dioxide, but almost all of it evaporates during baking. It is part of the lovely smell of baking bread.

faq.q: How does sourdough rise without packet yeast?
faq.a: Sourdough uses a starter, a bubbly mix of flour and water full of wild yeasts and bacteria from the flour and air. The yeasts raise the bread and the bacteria make it sour.

facts: Baker's yeast is the single-celled fungus Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Yeast ferments sugar into carbon dioxide and a small amount of alcohol.
Yeast cells are killed at around 60 degrees Celsius, early in baking.
